o: A beautiful configuration is a mountain (non-decreasing then non-increasing) with heights[i] ≤ maxHeights[i], maximizing the sum. Fixing the peak index i, the optimal configuration is forced: going left, heights decrease to the running minimum of maxHeights; going right, symmetrically. Computing this naively per peak is O(n²) — acceptable intuition, too slow for n = 10⁵. The standard trick defines left[i] = maximum sum of a non-decreasing prefix ending at i with heights[i] = maxHeights[i], computed with a monotonic stack: if p is the previous index with maxHeights[p] ≤ maxHeights[i] (previous smaller-or-equal), then left[i] = left[p] + maxHeights[i]·(i−p), else left[i] = maxHeights[i]·(i+1). Symmetrically right[i]. The answer is max(left[i] + right[i] − maxHeights[i]). Example 2: peak i=3 (height 9) gives left part 3+3+3+9=18, right part 9+2+2=13, minus overlap 9 → 22.
k: Fixing the peak, the optimal mountain is uniquely determined by running minima of maxHeights outward.
Monotonic stack recurrence left[i] = left[p] + h·(i−p) with p = previous index having maxHeights ≤ h gives O(n).
Answer = max over peaks of left[i] + right[i] − maxHeights[i].

a.i: Compute left[] scanning forward with a stack of indices maintaining increasing maxHeights; pop while stack top's height > current h, so the new previous-anchor p satisfies maxHeights[p] ≤ h. left[i] aggregates the rectangle from p+1..i at height h plus left[p]. Do the mirror pass for right[]. Combine at each index.
s: Forward pass with stack to fill left[].
Backward pass with stack to fill right[].
a.t: O(n) — each index pushed/popped from stacks once per pass

a.i: For each candidate peak i, walk left keeping the running minimum of maxHeights and summing, then walk right symmetrically. Direct translation of the definition; O(n²) but crystal clear and fine for small inputs.
s: For each peak i: sum = maxHeights[i], cur = maxHeights[i].
Walk right symmetrically; track the global max.

w: Use 64-bit sums: n = 10⁵ towers at height 10⁹ gives sums up to ~10¹⁴, overflowing 32-bit ints (and requiring BigInt care in JavaScript). Equal heights: popping on strict > (keeping equal heights on the stack) is fine since plateaus give identical results either way. Follow-up: Beautiful Towers I is the same problem with n ≤ 10³ where brute force passes; also related to maximal-rectangle-style stack recurrences.
